newsitem.title: USA: Pact reached to end San Francisco garbage strike.
newsitem.headline: Pact reached to end San Francisco garbage strike.

text.p: Striking garbage collectors and managers reached a tentative agreement on Friday to end a two-day-old strike for higher wages that caused trash to pile up at homes across San Francisco, officials said.

Mayor Willie Brown announced on Friday evening that a tentative settlement had been reached after two days of negotiations at City Hall between Norcal Waste Systems Inc. and union negotiators representing more than 500 striking garbage collectors.
It was the city's first strike by garbage collectors in 57 years.
A statement from Brown's office said terms of the agreement would not be announced until striking workers had voted on the agreement on Saturday.
It quoted Robert Morales, secretary-treasurer of Teamsters Local 350, as saying union negotiators would recommend workers approve the deal.
"The labor agreement has been reached, the vote will be tomorrow and we're very optimistic about it," Brown said.
He said striking workers should be back on the job by midday on Saturday and normal service should be restored throughout the city by Monday.
The statement from Brown's office quoted Norcal president Michael Sangiacomo as saying management was satisfied with the agreement.
The garbage collectors went on strike on Thursday in a dispute over a new labor contract. They had worked without a contract since Dec. 31.

Garbage company managers collected trash from hospitals, hotels, businesses and schools during the strike, but not from homes, where garbage started to pile up. City officials, fearing a prolonged strike could pose health risks, advised residents not to put garbage out on the curb.

Brown had said earlier he might declare a local state of emergency if the strike persisted and posed a threat to the health or public safety of San Franciscans. An emergency would have allowed Brown to call out city workers to pick up trash.
Union leaders called the strike after workers rejected the latest contract offer by Sunset Scavenger Co. and Golden Gate Disposal & Recycling Co., both Norcal subsidiaries.

The workers were seeking a three-year contract, an 80-cents-per-hour pay increase, an early retirement plan and improved health benefits. Before the strike the average garbage truck driver earned $20.58 per hour or $49,000 a year.
Norcal said before the strike that its latest proposal would boost workers' pay by 13.3 percent over five years and increase health care and pension benefits.
Union and company spokesmen could not immediately be reached for comment Friday evening.
